title: Αἴαντος καὶ Ἕκτορος ἀπειλαί
titleEn: The Taunts of Ajax and Hector — Iliad 13.748–837
part: The Taunts of Ajax and Hector (13.748–837)
about: Hector leaps down from his chariot, tells Polydamas to hold the chiefs where they are, and goes off through the Trojan ranks to look for Deiphobus, Helenus, Adamas and Asius. Some of them he finds dead by the ships and some wounded inside the wall, and on the left of the battle he finds Paris and reviles him. Paris answers that the companions Hector asks for are dead or have left the fight wounded, but that he is ready to follow wherever Hector leads. The Trojans advance behind Hector like a storm-blast breaking on the sea, and Ajax challenges him with a taunt. An eagle flies up on the right, and Hector answers Ajax with a threat in return. Both armies shout, and the din reaches the sky.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο Πουλυδάμας, ἅδε δ’ Ἕκτορι μῦθος ἀπήμων,
αὐτίκα δ’ ἐξ ὀχέων σὺν τεύχεσιν ἆλτο χαμᾶζε
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So spoke Polydamas, and it pleased Hector, the word, harmless,
and at once from the chariot, with his armour, he leapt to the ground,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So spoke Polydamas, and his harmless word pleased Hector, and at once he leapt from his chariot to the ground in his armour, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to Polydamas:
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο closes a speech, and φάτο is the unaugmented aorist of φημί. ἅδε is the aorist of ἁνδάνω ‘please’, also without augment, and it comes first, with the subject μῦθος ‘word’ and its adjective ἀπήμων ‘harmless’ (ἀ- + πῆμα ‘woe’) held back behind Ἕκτορι. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’; ὀχέων is a plural for one chariot, and χαμᾶζε is χαμαί ‘to the ground’ with the suffix -ζε of direction. In the third line μιν is Polydamas, whose advice ended the last part; the line is the stock introduction to a speech.

sentences.t:
Πουλυδάμα σὺ μὲν αὐτοῦ ἐρύκακε πάντας ἀρίστους,
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ κεῖσ’ εἶμι καὶ ἀντιόω πολέμοιο·
sentences.l:
“Polydamas, you on the spot hold back all the best,
but I shall go there and meet the war;
sentences.i: “Polydamas, you hold all the best men back here, but I shall go there and meet the war;
sentences.n: Πουλυδάμα is the vocative. ἐρύκακε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of ἐρύκω ‘hold back’, and αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, right here’, set against κεῖσ’ (κεῖσε) ‘there’. ἀντιόω is an epic by-form of ἀντιάω ‘meet’ and takes the genitive πολέμοιο, so ‘meet the war’ means to go and face the fighting. πάντας ἀρίστους ‘all the best’ are the chiefs whom Polydamas wanted called to council.

sentences.t: αἶψα δ’ ἐλεύσομαι αὖτις ἐπὴν εὖ τοῖς ἐπιτείλω.
sentences.l: Quickly I shall come again, when I have given them good charge.”
sentences.i: I shall quickly come back, once I have charged them properly.”
sentences.n: αἶψα ‘quickly’ and αὖτις ‘again, back’ are adverbs, and ἐλεύσομαι is the future of ἔρχομαι. ἐπήν is ἐπεὶ ἄν ‘when, once’, which takes the aorist subjunctive ἐπιτείλω: ‘when I have given them orders’. The verb is ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, lay a charge on’ with the dative τοῖς, ‘them’, the chiefs; the whole half-line stands in another speech earlier in the poem, and its English is kept. The unit closes Hector’s speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ὁρμήθη ὄρεϊ νιφόεντι ἐοικὼς
κεκλήγων, διὰ δὲ Τρώων πέτετ’ ἠδ’ ἐπικούρων.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and set off, to a snowy mountain likened,
shrieking, and through the Trojans he flew and the allies.
sentences.i: So he said, and set off like a snowy mountain, with a shrill cry, and flew through the Trojans and the allies.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα, καί is the formula ‘so he said, and’ for a speech that ends and an action that begins. ὁρμήθη is the aorist passive of ὁρμάω with active sense, ‘set off, sped’. ὄρεϊ νιφόεντι is the dative of ὄρος ‘mountain’ (epic ὄρεϊ for ὄρει) with νιφόεντι ‘snowy’, after ἐοικώς ‘like’; the Greek gives no point of likeness. κεκλήγων is the perfect participle of κλάζω ‘shriek’. πέτετο is the imperfect of πέτομαι ‘fly’, and ἐπίκουροι are the allies who came from outside Troy.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐς Πανθοΐδην ἀγαπήνορα Πουλυδάμαντα
πάντες ἐπεσσεύοντ’, ἐπεὶ Ἕκτορος ἔκλυον αὐδήν.
sentences.l:
And they to Panthous’-son, the man-cherishing Polydamas,
all rushed, when of Hector they heard the voice.
sentences.i: And they all rushed to Polydamas, son of Panthous, who prized manliness, when they heard Hector’s voice.
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ are the Trojans and allies of the last line. Πανθοΐδην is a patronymic in -ίδης, ‘son of Panthous’. ἀγαπήνορα, probably from ἀγαπάω ‘cherish’ and ἀνήρ ‘man’, is a stock epithet whose exact sense is not known; the Odyssey’s rendering ‘who prized manliness’ is kept in the English. ἐπεσσεύοντ’ is the imperfect middle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush to’, and ἔκλυον is the aorist of κλύω ‘hear’, with αὐδήν ‘voice’ as its object.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ Δηΐφοβόν τε βίην θ’ Ἑλένοιο ἄνακτος
Ἀσιάδην τ’ Ἀδάμαντα καὶ Ἄσιον Ὑρτάκου υἱὸν
φοίτα ἀνὰ προμάχους διζήμενος, εἴ που ἐφεύροι.
sentences.l:
But he Deiphobus and the might of lord Helenus,
Asius’-son Adamas, and Asius, Hyrtacus’ son,
went to and fro among the front-fighters, seeking, in case anywhere he might find them.
sentences.i: But he went to and fro among the foremost fighters, looking for Deiphobus and the might of lord Helenus, and Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus, in case he might find them anywhere.
sentences.n: The sentence holds its verb back: the four accusatives Δηΐφοβον, βίην Ἑλένοιο, Ἀδάμαντα and Ἄσιον are all objects of διζήμενος ‘seeking’ in line 760. βίην Ἑλένοιο ‘the might of Helenus’ is a periphrasis, the man spoken of through his strength. Ἀσιάδην is a patronymic, ‘son of Asius’, naming Adamas; the Asius of the next clause is another man, son of Hyrtacus. φοίτα is the imperfect of φοιτάω ‘go to and fro’, and εἴ που ἐφεύροι is an optative after a past tense, ‘in case he might find (them)’.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ εὗρ’ οὐκέτι πάμπαν ἀπήμονας οὐδ’ ἀνολέθρους·
sentences.l: And them he found no longer at all unharmed nor undestroyed;
sentences.i: But he found them no longer at all unharmed or free from destruction;
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ ‘but them’ takes up the four men just named, and εὗρ’ is the elided aorist εὗρε. ἀπήμονας ‘unharmed’ (ἀ- + πῆμα ‘woe’) is the house word for a man who has suffered no hurt; ἀνολέθρους is its neighbour, ‘without ὄλεθρος (destruction)’, so that the pair says one thing twice. With the negatives οὐκέτι and οὐδ’ the sense is that they are no longer whole, as the next lines explain. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν δὴ νηυσὶν ἔπι πρυμνῇσιν Ἀχαιῶν
χερσὶν ὑπ’ Ἀργείων κέατο ψυχὰς ὀλέσαντες,
οἳ δ’ ἐν τείχει ἔσαν βεβλημένοι οὐτάμενοί τε.
sentences.l:
But some indeed at the sterns of the ships of the Achaeans
beneath the hands of the Argives lay, having lost their souls,
and others within the wall were, struck and wounded.
sentences.i: Some of them lay at the sterns of the ships of the Achaeans, at the hands of the Argives, having lost their lives, and others were within the wall, struck and wounded.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οἳ μὲν δή … οἳ δ’ divides the four men’s fates into two kinds: dead, and wounded. νηυσὶν ἔπι πρυμνῇσιν is ἐπὶ νηυσὶ πρυμνῇσι, with the preposition after its noun and the epic dative plural; πρυμνῇσιν agrees with νηυσίν, ‘at the sterns of the ships’. κέατο is the epic third plural imperfect of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and ψυχὰς ὀλέσαντες is the aorist participle of ὄλλυμι, ‘having lost their lives’. βεβλημένοι ‘struck’ is a perfect passive participle and οὐτάμενοι ‘wounded’ an aorist one. ‘The wall’ is not named; it is probably Troy’s, but the Greek says only τείχει.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ τάχ’ εὗρε μάχης ἐπ’ ἀριστερὰ δακρυοέσσης
δῖον Ἀλέξανδρον Ἑλένης πόσιν ἠϋκόμοιο
θαρσύνονθ’ ἑτάρους καὶ ἐποτρύνοντα μάχεσθαι,
ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱστάμενος προσέφη αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσι·
sentences.l:
And him soon he found, on the left of tearful battle,
heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen,
cheering his companions and urging them on to fight,
and standing near he addressed him with shameful words:
sentences.i: Soon he found him, on the left of the tearful battle, heavenly Alexander, husband of fine-haired Helen, cheering his companions and urging them on to fight, and standing close by he spoke to him with shameful words:
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ ‘and him’ is Alexander (that is, Paris), who is named in the next line, and τάχ’ ‘soon’ with εὗρε ‘found’ ends the search of 760. ἐπ’ ἀριστερά is ‘on the left’, and δακρυοέσσης is the feminine genitive of δακρυόεις ‘tearful’, a stock epithet of battle. ἠϋκόμοιο ‘fine-haired’ agrees with Ἑλένης although it stands after πόσιν. θαρσύνονθ’ (θαρσύνοντα) and ἐποτρύνοντα are accusative participles on Ἀλέξανδρον, and ἑτάρους is the epic spelling of ἑταίρους. The subject of ἱστάμενος and προσέφη is Hector, who is not named here; αἰσχροῖς ἐπέεσσι is a dative of means.

sentences.l:
“Ill-Paris, best in form, woman-mad, deceiver,
where for you are Deiphobus and the might of lord Helenus,
and Asius’-son Adamas, and Asius, Hyrtacus’ son?
sentences.i: “Wretched Paris, fairest in looks, mad for women, deceiver, where are Deiphobus and the might of lord Helenus, and Adamas son of Asius, and Asius son of Hyrtacus?
sentences.n: The first line is the line with which Hector reviled the same man in Book 3: Δύσπαρι is a vocative with δυσ- ‘ill’ put before Πάρις as an insult, εἶδος is an accusative of respect (‘best in form’), and γυναιμανές ‘woman-mad’ and ἠπεροπευτά ‘deceiver’ are vocatives too. The question ποῦ τοι has a dative τοι ‘to you, for you’, which the English leaves implied. The four names are those of 758–759, so Hector asks after the very men he has just failed to find. Ἀσιάδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Asius’, and ἠδ’ is an epic ‘and’.

sentences.t: ποῦ δέ τοι Ὀθρυονεύς;
sentences.l: And where for you is Othryoneus?
sentences.i: And where is Othryoneus?
sentences.n: Another question with ποῦ τοι, now naming one man. Othryoneus is the ally from Cabesus whom Idomeneus killed earlier in this book (13.363), so Hector’s list takes in a man who is already dead. The question stops at the semicolon of the edition, a Greek question mark, in the middle of the line, and the answer begins in the same line.

sentences.t:
νῦν ὤλετο πᾶσα κατ’ ἄκρης
Ἴλιος αἰπεινή·
sentences.l:
now has perished, all of it, from the top down,
Ilios, steep;
sentences.i: Now all steep Ilios has perished from the top down.
sentences.n: νῦν ὤλετο ‘now has perished’ uses the aorist middle of ὄλλυμι for a state just reached. πᾶσα … Ἴλιος ‘the whole of Ilios’ takes the adjective αἰπεινή ‘steep’ after it, so that the city’s height is named last. κατ’ ἄκρης is ‘from the top down’ (ἄκρη ‘summit, citadel’), an idiom for ruin that begins at the height and leaves nothing. Hector speaks as though the city has already fallen.

sentences.t: νῦν τοι σῶς αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος.
sentences.l: now for you sure is steep destruction.”
sentences.i: Now steep destruction is certain for you.”
sentences.n: νῦν repeats the νῦν of the line before. σῶς is usually ‘safe, sound’; here it is ‘sure, certain’, the predicate of αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος ‘steep destruction’ (ruin pictured as a fall from a height), and τοι is again ‘for you’. The Odyssey has the same line of a different man’s ruin, and its English is kept. The unit closes Hector’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν Ἀλέξανδρος θεοειδής·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Alexander godlike-in-form:
sentences.i: Then Alexander, godlike in form, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπεν is the formula for a reply: προσέειπεν is the aorist of προσεῖπον ‘speak to’ with its epic uncontracted -εε-, and αὖτε ‘in turn’. Ἀλέξανδρος is Paris’ other name, which the poet uses here when Hector has just called him by the insult Δύσπαρι; θεοειδής ‘godlike in form’ (θεός + εἶδος) is his stock epithet. The line is the same as in Book 3 (3.58), and so is its English.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ ἐπεί τοι θυμὸς ἀναίτιον αἰτιάασθαι,
ἄλλοτε δή ποτε μᾶλλον ἐρωῆσαι πολέμοιο
μέλλω, ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ ἐμὲ πάμπαν ἀνάλκιδα γείνατο μήτηρ·
sentences.i: “Hector, since your heart is set on blaming the blameless, there may be some other time when I hold back from war more, for my mother did not bear even me without might at all;
sentences.n: ἐπεί τοι θυμὸς ἀναίτιον αἰτιάασθαι has no verb: supply ‘is set’. ἀναίτιον ‘blameless’ is the neuter used for a person, and αἰτιάασθαι is the uncontracted infinitive of αἰτιάομαι ‘blame’. ἐρωῆσαι ‘draw back’ takes the genitive πολέμοιο, and μέλλω with an infinitive says ‘I am likely, I am set to’: Paris grants that there may be times when he holds back, then gives his reason, that he is not a man without might. ἀνάλκιδα ‘without might’ is the house word; γείνατο is the unaugmented aorist of γείνομαι ‘bear’.

sentences.t:
ἐξ οὗ γὰρ παρὰ νηυσὶ μάχην ἤγειρας ἑταίρων,
ἐκ τοῦ δ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἐόντες ὁμιλέομεν Δαναοῖσι
νωλεμέως·
sentences.i: For ever since you stirred up the battle of our companions by the ships, we have been here mingling with the Danaans without pause;
sentences.n: ἐξ οὗ ‘from the time when’ is answered by ἐκ τοῦ ‘from that time’. ἤγειρας is the aorist of ἐγείρω ‘rouse’, and μάχην ἑταίρων is ‘the battle of the companions’, the fighting of Hector’s own men. ἐόντες is the participle of εἰμί, ‘being’, with ἐνθάδ’ ‘here’. ὁμιλέω with the dative Δαναοῖσι (epic -οισι) means ‘mingle with’, and in fighting ‘be engaged with’. νωλεμέως ‘unceasingly’ ends the unit at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἕταροι δὲ κατέκταθεν οὓς σὺ μεταλλᾷς.
sentences.l: and the companions were killed whom you ask after.
sentences.i: and the companions you are asking after have been killed.
sentences.n: ἕταροι is the epic spelling of ἑταῖροι. κατέκταθεν is the epic aorist passive of κατακτείνω, ‘were killed’, with -θεν in place of -θησαν. οὓς σὺ μεταλλᾷς is a relative clause on ἕταροι: μεταλλάω is ‘ask after’, and -ᾷς is the contracted second singular. Paris answers Hector’s questions one by one, the dead first.

sentences.t:
οἴω Δηΐφοβός τε βίη θ’ Ἑλένοιο ἄνακτος
οἴχεσθον, μακρῇσι τετυμμένω ἐγχείῃσιν
ἀμφοτέρω κατὰ χεῖρα·
sentences.i: Only Deiphobus and the might of lord Helenus have gone off, both of them struck in the hand by long spears;
sentences.n: οἴω is the dual of οἶος ‘alone, only’, ‘the two alone’; it is not the verb ὀΐω ‘I think’. The verb οἴχεσθον (οἴχομαι ‘be gone’) is dual too, because the two names make a pair, and τετυμμένω and ἀμφοτέρω are duals as well: τετυμμένω is the perfect participle of τύπτω ‘strike’, ‘both struck’. μακρῇσι … ἐγχείῃσιν is a dative of means in -ῃσι(ν). κατὰ χεῖρα is ‘in the hand’. ‘Have gone’ here means that the two have left the fighting.

sentences.t: φόνον δ’ ἤμυνε Κρονίων.
sentences.l: but slaughter the son of Cronus warded off.
sentences.i: but the son of Cronus warded off their slaughter.
sentences.n: ἤμυνε is the imperfect of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, with the accusative φόνον ‘slaughter’. Κρονίων ‘son of Cronus’ is Zeus, called only by his patronymic, as often. δ’ ‘but’ sets this against the wounds just named: they were hurt, but not killed.

sentences.t: νῦν δ’ ἄρχ’ ὅππῃ σε κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει·
sentences.l: But now lead on wherever heart and spirit bid you;
sentences.i: But now lead on, wherever your heart and spirit bid you;
sentences.n: νῦν δ’ ‘but now’ turns from what has happened to what is next. ἄρχ’ is the imperative ἄρχε ‘lead (the way)’, and ὅππῃ is ‘wherever, in whatever direction’ (a by-form of ὅπῃ). κραδίη θυμός τε ‘heart and spirit’ is a formula, and the verb κελεύει is singular for its two subjects. The same words stand in the Odyssey, where a host sends a guest wherever he wishes.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς δ’ ἐμμεμαῶτες ἅμ’ ἑψόμεθ’, οὐδέ τί φημι
ἀλκῆς δευήσεσθαι, ὅση δύναμίς γε πάρεστι.
sentences.l:
And we, eager, along with you will follow, and not at all, I say,
of might shall we fall short, as much as ability at least is at hand.
sentences.i: And we shall follow with you eagerly, and I say that we shall not fall short in any way of might, so far as our ability goes.
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς δ’ ‘and we’ is Paris and the men with him. ἐμμεμαῶτες is the perfect participle of ἐμμέμαα ‘be eager’, with the epic ending -ῶτες (Attic -ότες), and ἑψόμεθ’ is the future of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. οὐδέ τί φημι ‘and I say … not at all’ governs the future infinitive δευήσεσθαι ‘to lack, fall short of’ (the epic form of δεήσεσθαι from δέομαι) with the genitive ἀλκῆς ‘of might’. ὅση δύναμίς γε πάρεστι ‘as much as ability at least is at hand’ limits it. The same two lines stand in the Odyssey, and their English is kept.

sentences.t: πὰρ δύναμιν δ’ οὐκ ἔστι καὶ ἐσσύμενον πολεμίζειν.
sentences.l: and beyond ability it is not possible, even for one eager, to fight.”
sentences.i: but beyond one’s ability there is no fighting, however eager one is.”
sentences.n: πὰρ is παρά with its final vowel cut off before δύναμιν, ‘beyond ability’. οὐκ ἔστι, with ἔστι accented, means ‘it is not possible’, and the infinitive πολεμίζειν ‘to fight’ is the thing not possible. καὶ ἐσσύμενον ‘even (one) who is eager’ is an accusative participle of σεύομαι ‘rush’ that goes with the unnamed subject of the infinitive. The saying closes Paris’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν παρέπεισεν ἀδελφειοῦ φρένας ἥρως·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he talked round his brother’s wits, the hero;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the hero talked his brother’s mind round;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ has Alexander as its subject, and ἥρως ‘the hero’ is held back to the end of the line. ἀδελφειοῦ is the epic spelling of ἀδελφοῦ (‘brother’, as ἀδελφεόν elsewhere), and the brother is Hector. παρέπεισεν is the aorist of παραπείθω ‘talk round, win over’, with φρένας ‘wits’ as its object. The line is the same as in Book 7, where Agamemnon talks round Menelaus; only the persons change, so the English keeps the wording of the line and not its names.

sentences.t:
βὰν δ’ ἴμεν ἔνθα μάλιστα μάχη καὶ φύλοπις ἦεν
ἀμφί τε Κεβριόνην καὶ ἀμύμονα Πουλυδάμαντα
Φάλκην Ὀρθαῖόν τε καὶ ἀντίθεον Πολυφήτην
Πάλμύν τ’ Ἀσκάνιόν τε Μόρυν θ’ υἷ’ Ἱπποτίωνος,
sentences.l:
And they set out to go where most of all battle and battle-din was,
around Cebriones and blameless Polydamas,
Phalces and Orthaeus and godlike Polyphetes,
Palmys and Ascanius and Morys, the two sons of Hippotion,
sentences.i: And they set out to go where the battle and the din of battle were fiercest, around Cebriones and blameless Polydamas, Phalces and Orthaeus and godlike Polyphetes, Palmys and Ascanius and Morys, the sons of Hippotion,
sentences.n: βὰν δ’ ἴμεν ‘and they set out to go’: βάν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω (= ἔβησαν) and ἴμεν the epic infinitive of εἶμι ‘go’. ἔνθα μάλιστα ‘where most of all’ goes with μάχη καὶ φύλοπις ‘battle and the din of battle’ (ἦεν = ἦν). ἀμφί ‘around’ takes all the names that follow in the accusative. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is a stock epithet whose sense is not known, and ἀντίθεον is ‘godlike’. υἷ’ is υἷε, the dual of υἱός, usually taken as ‘the two sons’ (Ascanius and Morys); it could also be the singular υἷα.

sentences.t:
οἵ ῥ’ ἐξ Ἀσκανίης ἐριβώλακος ἦλθον ἀμοιβοὶ
ἠοῖ τῇ προτέρῃ·
sentences.l:
who from rich-soiled Ascania came as replacements
at the earlier dawn;
sentences.i: who had come from rich-soiled Ascania as replacements the dawn before;
sentences.n: οἵ ῥ’ ‘who’ points back to the leaders just named (ῥα is an epic particle). ἀμοιβοί is ‘in exchange, as a relief’: they came to take over from others. Ἀσκανίης ἐριβώλακος is ‘of rich-soiled Ascania’, ἐριβώλακος being the epic genitive of ἐριβῶλαξ. ἠοῖ τῇ προτέρῃ is a dative of time, ‘at the earlier dawn’ (ἠοῖ is the dative of ἠώς, and προτέρῃ agrees with it). The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τότε δὲ Ζεὺς ὦρσε μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l: but then Zeus roused them to fight.
sentences.i: but then Zeus roused them to fight.
sentences.n: τότε δὲ ‘but then’ contrasts the dawn before with this day. ὦρσε is the augmented aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’ (the unaugmented ὄρσε stands at 1.10), and μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ is an infinitive of purpose; the plural object ‘them’ is understood. The poet gives the new onset to Zeus.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἴσαν ἀργαλέων ἀνέμων ἀτάλαντοι ἀέλλῃ,
ἥ ῥά θ’ ὑπὸ βροντῆς πατρὸς Διὸς εἶσι πέδον δέ,
sentences.l:
And they went, equal to a blast of grievous winds,
which beneath the thunder of father Zeus goes to the ground,
sentences.i: And they came on like a storm of grievous winds, which sweeps down to the earth beneath the thunder of father Zeus,
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’ turns back to the Trojans; ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’ (= ἦσαν). ἀτάλαντοι ‘equal to’ takes the dative ἀέλλῃ, a word the house renders ‘blast’ in the literal English and ‘storm’ in the free English, and ἀργαλέων ἀνέμων ‘of grievous winds’ depends on it. ἥ ῥά θ’ ‘which indeed’ begins a relative clause, with ἥ the feminine relative and θ’ the epic τε of a general truth. ὑπὸ βροντῆς is ‘beneath the thunder’, and πέδον δέ is πέδον ‘ground’ with -δε of direction.

sentences.t:
θεσπεσίῳ δ’ ὁμάδῳ ἁλὶ μίσγεται, ἐν δέ τε πολλὰ
κύματα παφλάζοντα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης
κυρτὰ φαληριόωντα, πρὸ μέν τ’ ἄλλ’, αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ ἄλλα·
sentences.i: and with a wondrous uproar mingles with the sea, and in the sea there are many waves of the loud-roaring sea, seething, arched, white-flecked, some in front and others after them;
sentences.n: The subject is still the storm-blast. θεσπεσίῳ ὁμάδῳ is ‘with wondrous uproar’ (ὁμαδός ‘uproar’, the root of the Odyssey’s ὁμάδησαν), and ἁλί is the dative of ἅλς ‘sea’ after μίσγεται ‘mingles with’. ἐν δέ τε πολλά starts a new clause with no verb: ‘and in it there are many waves’. παφλάζοντα ‘seething’, κυρτά ‘arched’ and φαληριόωντα ‘white-flecked’ (formed on φαληρός ‘white-spotted’) all describe κύματα. πρὸ μέν τ’ ἄλλ’, αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ ἄλλα ‘some in front, but others upon (after) them’ sets up the Trojan comparison.

sentences.t:
ὣς Τρῶες πρὸ μὲν ἄλλοι ἀρηρότες, αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ ἄλλοι,
χαλκῷ μαρμαίροντες ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν ἕποντο.
sentences.l:
So the Trojans, some in front, fitted close, but others after,
gleaming with bronze, together with the leaders followed.
sentences.i: So the Trojans, some ranged in front and others behind, gleaming with bronze, followed along with their leaders.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the comparison, and the Trojans fall into the same pattern as the waves: πρὸ μὲν ἄλλοι … αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ ἄλλοι ‘some in front … but others after’ repeats πρὸ μέν τ’ ἄλλ’, αὐτὰρ ἐπ’ ἄλλα. ἀρηρότες is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit together’, here ‘fitted close’ in ranks. μαρμαίροντες is ‘gleaming’, and ἅμ’ ἡγεμόνεσσιν ἕποντο ‘followed along with their leaders’ uses the epic dative plural -εσσιν and the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ἡγεῖτο βροτολοιγῷ ἶσος Ἄρηϊ
Πριαμίδης·
sentences.l:
And Hector led them, equal to mortal-ruining Ares,
Priam’s-son;
sentences.i: And Hector, son of Priam, led them, the equal of Ares, the ruin of mortals;
sentences.n: ἡγεῖτο is the imperfect of ἡγέομαι ‘lead’. Ἕκτωρ … Πριαμίδης ‘Hector … Priam’s son’ is split by the epithet phrase βροτολοιγῷ ἶσος Ἄρηϊ ‘equal to Ares’; βροτολοιγός, from βροτός ‘mortal’ and λοιγός ‘ruin’, is ‘mortal-ruining’ in the literal English and ‘the ruin of mortals’ in the free English, as at 11.295, where the same words are used of Hector. Πριαμίδης is a patronymic.

sentences.t:
πρόσθεν δ’ ἔχεν ἀσπίδα πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην
ῥινοῖσιν πυκινήν, πολλὸς δ’ ἐπελήλατο χαλκός·
sentences.l:
and in front he held his shield, equal on every side,
solid with hides, and much bronze had been driven on;
sentences.i: and in front of him he held his shield, equal on every side, solid with hides, and much bronze had been hammered on;
sentences.n: πρόσθεν ‘in front’ goes with ἔχεν, the unaugmented imperfect of ἔχω (Attic εἶχεν); the first line is the line that describes Deiphobus’ shield at 13.157. πάντοσ’ ἐΐσην ‘equal on every side’ means a round shield. ῥινοῖσιν ‘with hides’ is a dative of material, and πυκινήν ‘solid’ agrees with ἀσπίδα. ἐπελήλατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐπελαύνω ‘drive on’, said of metal beaten out in layers, with the subject πολλὸς χαλκός ‘much bronze’; the hides are covered with bronze.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κροτάφοισι φαεινὴ σείετο πήληξ.
sentences.l: and around his temples the shining helmet was shaken.
sentences.i: and about his temples the shining helmet shook.
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κροτάφοισι ‘and about his temples’: ἀμφί governs the dative, οἱ is ‘his’ (the dative of the person), and κροτάφοισι is the epic dative plural of κρόταφος ‘temple’. φαεινή ‘shining’ and πήληξ ‘helmet’ are the house words. σείετο is the imperfect passive of σείω ‘shake’, the helmet tossing as he moves.

sentences.t:
πάντῃ δ’ ἀμφὶ φάλαγγας ἐπειρᾶτο προποδίζων,
εἴ πώς οἱ εἴξειαν ὑπασπίδια προβιβῶντι·
sentences.l:
On every side around the battle-lines he made trial, stepping forward,
if in some way they would yield to him, as he strode forward under the shield;
sentences.i: He tried the battle-lines on every side, advancing step by step, to see whether they would somehow give way to him as he strode forward under the shield;
sentences.n: πάντῃ ‘on every side’ goes with ἀμφί ‘around’ and φάλαγγας ‘battle-lines’. ἐπειρᾶτο is the imperfect middle of πειράω ‘try, make trial’, and προποδίζων ‘stepping forward’ is the verb used of Deiphobus at 13.158. εἴ πώς οἱ εἴξειαν is an optative after a past tense, ‘if somehow they would give way to him’, with εἴξειαν the aorist optative of εἴκω ‘yield’. ὑπασπίδια ‘under the shield’ is an adverb, and προβιβῶντι ‘as he strode forward’ is the dative participle of the lengthened προβιβάω.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ σύγχει θυμὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l: but he did not confound the heart in the breasts of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: but he did not throw the heart in the Achaeans’ breasts into confusion.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ οὐ ‘but not’ gives the result of Hector’s trial: the lines did not give way. σύγχει is the imperfect of συγχέω ‘confound, throw into confusion’, unaugmented and in a contracted form, with θυμόν as its object. ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘in the breasts’, and Ἀχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans’ comes last, so the sentence ends on the men whose courage holds.

sentences.t: Αἴας δὲ πρῶτος προκαλέσσατο μακρὰ βιβάσθων·
sentences.l: But Ajax first challenged him, taking long strides:
sentences.i: But Ajax was the first to challenge him, taking long strides:
sentences.n: Αἴας without a further name is the great Ajax, son of Telamon, whose fighting beside the other Ajax the last part described. πρῶτος ‘first’ means he was the first to answer Hector. προκαλέσσατο is the aorist middle of προκαλέω ‘call out, challenge’ (the object, Hector, is understood). μακρὰ βιβάσθων ‘taking long strides’ is the present participle in the lengthened form -βάσθων (compare βιβάς).

sentences.t: δαιμόνιε σχεδὸν ἐλθέ·
sentences.l: “Strange man, come near;
sentences.i: “Strange man, come near;
sentences.n: δαιμόνιε is a vocative of address whose force is not settled (‘strange one’, ‘driven by something beyond yourself’); the house ‘Strange man’ is kept, and here it is a challenge. ἐλθέ is the aorist imperative of ἔρχομαι, and σχεδόν ‘near’ is an adverb. The ano teleia ends the call before the question.

sentences.t:
τί ἢ δειδίσσεαι αὔτως
Ἀργείους;
sentences.l:
why then do you frighten, just so,
the Argives?
sentences.i: why try to frighten the Argives to no purpose?
sentences.n: τί ἢ ‘why then?’ is a question with an emphatic ἤ. δειδίσσεαι is the second person singular of δειδίσσομαι ‘try to frighten’, with the uncontracted ending -εαι (Attic -ῃ). αὔτως is ‘just so’, that is ‘for nothing, to no purpose’, and Ἀργείους ‘the Argives’ opens the next line.

sentences.t:
οὔ τοί τι μάχης ἀδαήμονές εἰμεν,
ἀλλὰ Διὸς μάστιγι κακῇ ἐδάμημεν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
We are not at all unacquainted with battle,
but by the evil whip of Zeus we were overcome, we Achaeans.
sentences.i: We are not strangers to battle, but we Achaeans were overcome by the evil whip of Zeus.
sentences.n: οὔ τοί τι ‘not at all’, with the particle τοι ‘you know’. ἀδαήμονες ‘unacquainted’ takes the genitive μάχης ‘with battle’, and εἰμεν is the epic first plural of εἰμί (Attic ἐσμέν). Διὸς μάστιγι κακῇ ‘by the evil whip of Zeus’ is a dative of cause, and ἐδάμημεν is the aorist passive of δάμνημι ‘overcome’; the phrase is the same as at 12.37. Ajax’s claim is that Zeus, not Hector, has beaten the Achaeans, and Ἀχαιοί stands last in apposition to the verb’s ‘we’.

sentences.t:
ἦ θήν πού τοι θυμὸς ἐέλπεται ἐξαλαπάξειν
νῆας·
sentences.l:
Truly, I suppose, your heart hopes to plunder utterly
the ships;
sentences.i: No doubt your heart hopes to plunder the ships;
sentences.n: ἦ θήν πού τοι is ‘truly, I suppose, your’: θήν is a particle of assertion, που ‘I suppose’, and τοι is the dative ‘to you, your’. θυμός ‘heart’ is the subject of ἐέλπεται (ἔλπομαι ‘hope’, with the epic doubled ε), which takes the future infinitive ἐξαλαπάξειν ‘to plunder utterly’, the house word of 1.129. The object νῆας ‘ships’ begins the second line, and the ano teleia ends the clause.

sentences.t: ἄφαρ δέ τε χεῖρες ἀμύνειν εἰσὶ καὶ ἡμῖν.
sentences.l: and at once hands to defend are ours also.
sentences.i: but we too have hands that are quick to defend.
sentences.n: ἄφαρ is ‘at once’, here ‘ready at once’; δέ τε is ‘but’ with the epic τε. χεῖρες ἀμύνειν εἰσί ‘there are hands to ward off’ has an infinitive of purpose, ἀμύνειν, and καὶ ἡμῖν ‘to us also’ is a dative of possession. Ajax answers Hector’s hope with a plain statement of readiness.

sentences.t:
ἦ κε πολὺ φθαίη εὖ ναιομένη πόλις ὑμὴ
χερσὶν ὑφ’ ἡμετέρῃσιν ἁλοῦσά τε περθομένη τε.
sentences.l:
Truly your well-inhabited city would be first by far,
beneath our hands taken and being sacked.
sentences.i: Surely your well-peopled city will be taken and sacked beneath our hands far sooner.
sentences.n: ἦ κε πολὺ φθαίη: ἦ is ‘truly’, κε the particle of a potential optative, πολύ ‘by far’, and φθαίη the aorist optative of φθάνω ‘be first, get in ahead’. The comparison is left unsaid: your city would be taken before you take our ships. ναιομένη is the present participle passive of ναίω, so εὖ ναιομένη is ‘well-inhabited’, and ὑμή is the epic ‘your’ (ὑμός). ἁλοῦσα is the aorist participle of ἁλίσκομαι ‘be taken’ and περθομένη the present passive of πέρθω ‘sack’. The second line is the line of Book 2 (2.374), with the same English.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ φημὶ σχεδὸν ἔμμεναι ὁππότε φεύγων
ἀρήσῃ Διὶ πατρὶ καὶ ἄλλοις ἀθανάτοισι
θάσσονας ἰρήκων ἔμεναι καλλίτριχας ἵππους,
οἵ σε πόλιν δ’ οἴσουσι κονίοντες πεδίοιο.
sentences.l:
And for you yourself I say it is near, when, fleeing,
you will pray to father Zeus and the other immortals
that your fair-maned horses be swifter than hawks,
which will carry you to the city, raising dust over the plain.”
sentences.i: And for you yourself I say that the time is near when, in flight, you will pray to father Zeus and the other immortals that your fair-maned horses may be swifter than hawks, to carry you to the city as they raise dust over the plain.”
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ αὐτῷ φημὶ σχεδὸν ἔμμεναι has no stated subject: ‘I say it is near (the time) when’. ἀρήσῃ is an aorist subjunctive of ἀράομαι ‘pray’ (Homer can drop κε after ὁππότε), and what is prayed for stands in an accusative and infinitive: θάσσονας ἰρήκων ἔμεναι … ἵππους ‘that the horses be swifter than hawks’, with θάσσων the comparative of ταχύς and ἰρήκων a genitive of comparison. οἵ ‘which’ points to the horses; οἴσουσι is the future of φέρω, πόλιν δ’ is πόλιν with -δε ‘to the city’, κονίοντες is ‘raising dust’, and πεδίοιο ‘over the plain’ is a genitive of the ground crossed. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα οἱ εἰπόντι ἐπέπτατο δεξιὸς ὄρνις
αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης·
sentences.l:
So then, to him as he spoke, there flew up on the right a bird,
an eagle, high-flying;
sentences.i: As soon as he had spoken, a bird flew up on the right, a high-flying eagle;
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα οἱ εἰπόντι ‘so then, to him as he spoke’ has the dative participle εἰπόντι (aorist of εἶπον) with οἱ ‘to him’, that is Ajax. The line is the same as in the Odyssey at 15.160, where it introduces another eagle, and the English is kept. ἐπέπτατο is the aorist of ἐπιπέτομαι ‘fly up’. δεξιός ‘on the right’ was the lucky side for an omen, and ὄρνις … αἰετός ὑψιπέτης names the bird twice, first generally and then as ‘a high-flying eagle’.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ἴαχε λαὸς Ἀχαιῶν
θάρσυνος οἰωνῷ·
sentences.l:
and in answer shouted the people of the Achaeans,
emboldened by the bird of omen;
sentences.i: and the army of the Achaeans shouted in answer, emboldened by the bird of omen;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ δ’ ἴαχε is tmesis for ἐπιάχω ‘shout in answer’, and ἴαχε is the aorist of ἰάχω. λαὸς Ἀχαιῶν is ‘the people of the Achaeans’ in the literal English and ‘the army’ in the free English. θάρσυνος is a rare adjective from θάρσος ‘courage’, taken as ‘emboldened’, with the dative οἰωνῷ; οἰωνός can mean the bird or the sign it gives, and the house rendering ‘bird of omen’ keeps both.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἀμείβετο φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ·
sentences.l: and he answered, glorious Hector:
sentences.i: and glorious Hector answered:
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ marks the change of speaker. ἀμείβετο is the imperfect middle of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, the verb of the reply formulas. φαίδιμος Ἕκτωρ ‘glorious Hector’ is a stock epithet, translated the same way each time. The ano teleia opens the speech.

sentences.t: Αἶαν ἁμαρτοεπὲς βουγάϊε ποῖον ἔειπες·
sentences.l: “Ajax, errant in speech, braggart, what sort of thing you have said;
sentences.i: “Ajax, you who speak wide of the mark, you braggart, what a thing you have said!
sentences.n: Αἶαν is the vocative of Αἴας. ἁμαρτοεπές, from ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’ and ἔπος ‘word’, means ‘missing in speech’, speaking wide of the mark. βουγάϊε is a vocative of abuse whose meaning is not known; ‘braggart’ is the usual guess, and the Odyssey has the word once, as an insult (18.79). ποῖον ἔειπες ‘what sort of thing you have said’ is an exclamation in the form of a question, and ἔειπες is the epic aorist of λέγω (= εἶπες).

sentences.t:
εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼν οὕτω γε Διὸς πάϊς αἰγιόχοιο
εἴην ἤματα πάντα, τέκοι δέ με πότνια Ἥρη,
τιοίμην δ’ ὡς τίετ’ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἀπόλλων,
ὡς νῦν ἡμέρη ἥδε κακὸν φέρει Ἀργείοισι
πᾶσι μάλ’,
sentences.l:
if only I, so surely, were the son of aegis-bearing Zeus
for all my days, and lady Hera had borne me,
and were honoured as Athena and Apollo are honoured,
as surely this day brings evil to the Argives,
all, every one,
sentences.i: If only I were the son of aegis-bearing Zeus for all my days, and lady Hera had borne me, and I were honoured as Athena and Apollo are honoured, as surely as this day brings evil to the Argives, to every one of them,
sentences.n: A wish: εἰ γὰρ … εἴην ‘if only I were’, with τέκοι (aorist optative of τίκτω ‘bear’) and τιοίμην (optative of τίω ‘honour’) also in the wish. οὕτω γε ‘so surely’ answers ὡς νῦν ‘as surely as now’ in the fourth line, so that the wish is a kind of oath: as surely as this day brings evil, so surely may I be a son of Zeus. πάϊς is ‘child’, here ‘son’, and αἰγιόχοιο is the epic genitive of αἰγίοχος ‘aegis-bearing’ (meaning disputed). The lines about Athena and Apollo are those of Hector’s own wish at 8.538–541. πᾶσι μάλ’ ‘to every one’ ends the unit in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ σὺ τοῖσι πεφήσεαι, αἴ κε ταλάσσῃς
μεῖναι ἐμὸν δόρυ μακρόν, ὅ τοι χρόα λειριόεντα
δάψει·
sentences.i: and you will be slain among them, if you can bring yourself to await my long spear, which will tear your lily-like skin;
sentences.n: ἐν δὲ … τοῖσι ‘and among them’ means among the Argives, and πεφήσεαι is the future passive of the reduplicated stem πεφη- ‘be slain’ (epic uncontracted -εαι). αἴ κε ταλάσσῃς is εἰ ἄν with an aorist subjunctive of the epic verb ταλάσσω, from the root of τλῆναι, ‘bring yourself to’; it takes μεῖναι ‘to await’. In ὅ τοι χρόα λειριόεντα δάψει, ὅ is the neuter relative (the spear), τοι is ‘your’, χρόα is the accusative of χρώς ‘skin’, λειριόεντα ‘lily-like’ is the word used of the cicadas’ voice in Book 3, and δάψει is the future of δάπτω ‘tear’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ Τρώων κορέεις κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνοὺς
δημῷ καὶ σάρκεσσι πεσὼν ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.l:
but the dogs and birds of the Trojans you will sate
with fat and with flesh, having fallen by the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: and you will glut the Trojans’ dogs and birds with your fat and flesh, fallen by the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: ἀτάρ ‘but, and yet’ opens the second threat. Τρώων … κύνας ἠδ’ οἰωνούς is ‘the dogs and birds of the Trojans’, with Τρώων going with both nouns, and the pair is the object of κορέεις, the future of κορέννυμι ‘sate, glut’. δημῷ καὶ σάρκεσσι ‘with fat and flesh’ are datives of means, and πεσών ‘having fallen’ is the aorist participle of πίπτω. These lines closely resemble a speech in Book 8 (8.379), but there τις Τρώων is ‘one of the Trojans’ and here the genitive cannot be partitive, so the English differs in its first line. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἡγήσατο· τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο
ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ, ἐπὶ δ’ ἴαχε λαὸς ὄπισθεν.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, he led the way; and they together followed
with wondrous din, and the people shouted in answer behind.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and led the way, and they followed along together with a wondrous din, and the army shouted in answer from behind.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας ἡγήσατο is a formula, with ἡγήσατο the aorist of ἡγέομαι ‘lead the way’; the subject, Hector, is not named. τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο ‘and they followed along’ has the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι, and ἠχῇ θεσπεσίῃ ‘with wondrous din’ is a dative of manner with the epic ending -ῃ. ἐπὶ δ’ ἴαχε is tmesis again, ‘and shouted in answer’, with λαὸς ὄπισθεν ‘the people behind’.

sentences.t:
Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ἐπίαχον, οὐδὲ λάθοντο
ἀλκῆς, ἀλλ’ ἔμενον Τρώων ἐπιόντας ἀρίστους.
sentences.l:
And the Argives from the other side shouted in answer, and did not forget
might, but awaited the best of the Trojans coming on.
sentences.i: And the Argives shouted from the other side and did not forget their might, but stood to await the best of the Trojans as they came on.
sentences.n: Ἀργεῖοι δ’ ἑτέρωθεν ‘and the Argives on the other side’; ἐπίαχον is a past tense of the verb of ἴαχε in line 834, ‘shouted in answer’. οὐδὲ λάθοντο ἀλκῆς ‘did not forget might’ is the aorist middle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’ with the genitive, ἀλκή being ‘might’ as before. ἔμενον Τρώων ἐπιόντας ἀρίστους is ‘awaited the best of the Trojans coming on’: μένω with an accusative means ‘await’, Τρώων is partitive, and ἐπιόντας is the accusative participle of ἔπειμι ‘come on’ agreeing with ἀρίστους.

sentences.t: ἠχὴ δ’ ἀμφοτέρων ἵκετ’ αἰθέρα καὶ Διὸς αὐγάς.
sentences.l: And the din of both reached the aether and the glare of Zeus.
sentences.i: And the din of both sides reached the upper air and the glare of Zeus.
sentences.n: ἠχή ‘din’ is the subject, and ἀμφοτέρων ‘of both’ means of both armies. ἵκετ’ is the unaugmented ἵκετο of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’, with two objects, αἰθέρα ‘upper air’ (αἰθήρ) and Διὸς αὐγάς. αὐγή is the house ‘glare’ (as at 2.456 and 13.244), and ‘the glare of Zeus’ is the bright sky. The part closes on the noise of the two lines meeting.
